statement: Equilateral triangle $ABP$ is drawn inside regular pentagon $ABCDE$, so that $P$ lies in the interior of the pentagon. What is the degree measure of $\angle CPD$?

choices.misconception: I found angle PCD = 108 - 66 = 42 and stopped there, giving an angle at C instead of the angle at P.
I found angle PBC = 108 - 60 = 48 and gave that, which is the angle at B, not at P.
I found the base angle BCP = (180 - 48)/2 = 66 of isosceles triangle BCP and gave that.
I assumed PC = PD, so I made both base angles of triangle PCD equal to 42 and got 180 - 84 = 96. In fact P is on the line of symmetry through D, so PC = PE.

hints: Each interior angle of a regular pentagon is $108^\circ$. Look at triangle $PBC$.
Since $BP = BA = BC$, triangle $PBC$ is isosceles. Find its angles, then work in triangle $PCD$, using the pentagon's line of symmetry through $D$.
$\angle PBC = 48^\circ$, so $\angle BCP = 66^\circ$ and $\angle PCD = 42^\circ$. The symmetry line through $D$ and $P$ bisects $\angle CDE$, so $\angle PDC = 54^\circ$.

solutions.reliable: Interior angles of a regular pentagon are $108^\circ$. Since $ABP$ is equilateral, $BP = AB = BC$ and $\angle PBC = 108^\circ - 60^\circ = 48^\circ$. Triangle $BCP$ is isosceles with apex $48^\circ$, so $\angle BCP = (180^\circ - 48^\circ)/2 = 66^\circ$ and $\angle PCD = 108^\circ - 66^\circ = 42^\circ$. The perpendicular bisector of $AB$ is a line of symmetry of the pentagon passing through $D$, and $P$ lies on it because $PA = PB$. So $DP$ bisects $\angle CDE$ and $\angle PDC = 54^\circ$. In triangle $PCD$, $\angle CPD = 180^\circ - 42^\circ - 54^\circ = 84^\circ$. The transferable idea: equal lengths make isosceles triangles, and a figure's symmetry line hands you a bisected angle.
